# Morajātaka (Ja 159)

**ID:** Ja 159
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)
**Collection:** Suttas-Late-1
**Title (Pali):** Morajātaka
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** The Peacock
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/ja159
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0513m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Morajātaka* (Ja 159) is a canonical Jātaka tale belonging to the *Ekanipāta* of the Pali Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. In this narrative, the Bodhisatta is born as a golden peacock who secures protection from harm and hunters by reciting verses each morning and evening in praise of the rising and setting sun, the Buddhas, and their awakening [Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014; Eliot 1921; Schmithausen; SuttaCentral]. These verses constitute the *Mora Paritta*, an authorized protective chant in the Theravada tradition used to avert misfortune and danger; the peacock is captured only when distracted by the cries of a peahen, leading him to neglect his daily recitation [Appleton 2010; Crosby 2014; Eliot 1921]. In early Buddhist visual culture, the story is identified among the narrative reliefs at Amaravati under the theme of the peacock preaching the Dhamma [Francis 2002].

Within the Pali textual corpus, DharmaNexus detects extensive text reuse between Ja 159 and the commentary tradition, recording eleven matches with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* and five matches with the *Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā* of the *Aṅguttara Nikāya* [DharmaNexus]. Beyond the Pali tradition, modern scholars note that the verses and core narrative of the *Morajātaka* represent an ancient textual core underlying the northern Buddhist *rakṣā* tradition, specifically the *Mahāmāyūrī* (*Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī*), which was later incorporated into the *Pañcarakṣā* [Schmithausen; Skilling; The Bajaur collection; Winternitz 1933]. DharmaNexus corroborates this cross-language relationship through automated alignments between Ja 159 and the Tibetan translation of the *Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī* (D0559) [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā (Dutiyo bhāgo) (Atk S0513a2) (§3.1–4.6 ↔ §173–177); Aṅguttaranikāye Ekakanipāta-aṭṭhakathā (Atk S0401a) (§2.6–4.6 ↔ §132–141)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): རིག་སྔགས་ཀྱི་རྒྱལ་མོ་རྨ་བྱ་ཆེན་མོ། (mahāmayūrīvidyārājñī) (D0559) [bo]

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral record for ja159 — Canonical catalog data, English title, and opening blurb.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus database alignment for Ja 159 — Text reuse data with the Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā, Aṅguttaranikāya-aṭṭhakathā, and Tibetan Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī.
- [Appleton 2010] Naomi Appleton, Jātaka Stories in Theravāda Buddhism: Narrating the Bodhisatta Path (2010) — Discussion of the Mora Jātaka verses as a Bodhisatta-composed paritta in praise of the sun and the wise.
- [Crosby 2014] Kate Crosby, Theravada Buddhism: Continuity, Diversity, and Identity (2014) — Contextualization of the Mora Jātaka as a paritta recited for protection and the story of the peacock forgetting recitation.
- [Eliot 1921] Charles Eliot, Hinduism and Buddhism: An Historical Sketch, Vol. III (1921) — Note on the peacock escaping danger through daily recitation of a hymn to the sun and past Buddhas.
- [Francis 2002] Francis N. J., Buddhist Art, Religion and Society at Amaravati (2002) — Attestation of the Mora Jātaka relief at Amaravati.
- [Schmithausen] Lambert Schmithausen, Maitrī and Magic — Analysis of the golden peacock's solar and Buddha invocations and connection to the Mahāmāyūrī spell tradition.
- [Skilling] Peter Skilling, Jātaka and Paññāsa-jātaka in South-East Asia — Identification of Jātaka 159 at the heart of the Mahāmāyūrī-vidyārājñī in the Pañcarakṣā.
- [The Bajaur collection] The Bajaur collection: A new collection of Kharoṣṭhī manuscripts — Discussion of the Mahāmāyūrī's ancient core going back to a text related to the Morajātaka.
- [Winternitz 1933] Maurice Winternitz, History of Indian Literature, Vol. II (1933) — Tracing the Mahā-Mayūrī dhāraṇī back to the verses of Mora-Jātaka No. 159.
